metadata.summary: This expert statement reviews current ocular proton therapy practices, including clinical indications, tumor imaging and delineation, treatment planning, beam delivery, quality assurance, and care after treatment. It examines reported clinical outcomes and complications, compares radiation modalities, and identifies priorities for future technology and research. Its clinical evidence largely comes from established dedicated ocular treatment systems, so the authors caution against assuming equivalent outcomes with other beam qualities.

target_population: Patients receiving primary, salvage, or adjuvant ocular treatment
Adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients with UM
therapeutic_areas: brachytherapy using ruthenium-106 (Ru-106) or iodine-125 (I-125) plaques

prevention: Assess dose-volume histograms and select planning and delivery techniques that limit exposure of the macula and optic disc or nerve. Reports identify the macular volume and optic nerve length receiving 50% of the total dose (“V50%” or »28-30 Gray equivalent) as independent predictors of vision loss.

Consider gaze angle, lateral margins, aperture shape, distal range, and compensators or wedges when optimizing normal-tissue dose. Relatively sparing either the macula or optic disc may benefit vision even when the other receives a higher dose.

toxicities.event: Eyelid inflammation, irritation, erythema, and scarring
prevention: Choose the gaze angle and retract the eyelid systematically to reduce eyelid irradiation.

For small and medium tumors, eyelid retraction outside the field can be achieved through retractor selection, head tilt, and chair rotation. For larger tumors, full upper-eyelid retraction is preferred; transpalpebral treatment is an alternative.

recognition: Keratinization of the upper palpebral conjunctiva
prevention: Optimize gaze angle and eyelid retraction. For larger tumors, fully retracting the upper eyelid is preferred to limit keratinization; transpalpebral treatment may be used instead.
Retract eyelids outside the treatment field when feasible.
Gaze angle may be optimized to reduce exposure of the lacrimal gland and tear duct.
Adjust lens dose during planning to limit cataract risk.

management.actions: Use antiVEGF; laser treatment can be given once the ischemic retina has reattached.

prevention: Use dose-volume histogram assessment and adjust ciliary body and optic disc or nerve dose during planning to reduce risk.

recognition: Neovascular proliferation in the anterior segment
prevention: Some teams give prophylactic anti-VEGF therapy to reduce anterior-segment neovascularization.
Evaluate retinal dose and optimize treatment planning to limit exposure of critical structures.

management.actions: anti-VEGF therapy may be used in an attempt to preserve vision and microcirculation.

prevention: Evaluate macular dose during planning; a notched aperture can reduce dose to the macula.
Assess optic disc and nerve dose during planning. Notched apertures and wedge filters can reduce exposure to these structures.

recognition: Inflammatory response of the irradiated tumor

management.actions: Treat the irradiated tumor with laser ablation or transscleral or transretinal ablation.

prevention: Antiangiogenic therapy can prevent this syndrome.

management.actions: Depending on the circumstances, steroids, anti-VEGF therapy, vitrectomy, or endoresection can be used; enucleation is sometimes necessary.

prevention: Planning and delivery strategies that reduce critical-structure dose may limit sequelae.

recognition: An inflammatory tumor response that resembles recurrence

toxicities.incidence: Generally rare among severe radiation toxicities
prevention: Include the limbus and limbal stem cells in systematic critical-structure dose assessment.

toxicities.incidence: Generally rare among severe radiation toxicities
recognition: Necrosis of the eyelid or sclera

toxicities.incidence: Generally rare among severe radiation toxicities

prevention: Experienced ophthalmologic assessment and clip placement help avoid surgical pitfalls.

recognition: Conjunctival granuloma associated with a tantalum marker

prophylaxis.recommendation: Some teams use prophylactic anti-VEGF therapy to reduce anterior-segment neovascularization, for example, 1£/2 months for 6 months then 1£/3 months.
Antiangiogenic therapy can prevent toxic tumor syndrome.

therapies_index.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
therapies_index.mechanism: A conformal proton dose distribution can cover the tumor while limiting exposure of nearby ocular structures; beam fall-off and penumbra affect that sparing.
approved_indications: Treatment of uveal melanoma (UM) and other ocular tumors.

The review reports particle-beam treatment for UM, conjunctival tumors, choroidal metastases, hemangiomas, other vascular tumors, macular degeneration, and retinoblastomas, given as primary, salvage, or adjuvant treatment with combined modality therapy.
therapies_index.administration: Treatment uses a planned gaze direction, a shaped proton field, and image-guided positioning when tantalum markers are present. A United States cost-analysis study assessed a short course of 4-5 fractions.
key_toxicities: Eyelid inflammation and irritation, permanent eyelash loss, scleral telangiectasias, tear-duct occlusion, dry eyes, and cataracts.
Pseudorecurrence, neovascular proliferation, secondary glaucoma, retinopathy, maculopathy, and optic neuropathy.
Generally rare severe radiation effects include corneal limbal stem cell failure, eyelid or scleral necrosis, and exudative retinal detachment.
Anterior eye complications are more common with proton beam delivery than with other radiation modalities.
monitoring: Evaluate dose-volume measures for critical structures, including macula volume and optic nerve length receiving 50% of the total dose.
Monitor eye position during irradiation with a camera.

therapies_index.name: a second course of OPT
approved_indications: Salvage treatment of recurrent UM; the document reports outcomes after UM reirradiation.

therapies_index.name: proton therapy
approved_indications: Retreatment of local failures in UM and conjunctival tumors.

therapies_index.name: brachytherapy using ruthenium-106 (Ru-106) or iodine-125 (I-125) plaques
approved_indications: Irradiation of UM; the cited comparisons generally involve tumors with a smaller base and/or height or tumors farther from the optic disc and macula than those treated with protons.

therapies_index.name: Ru-106
approved_indications: Plaque irradiation of UM in the document’s comparison of radiation modalities.

therapies_index.name: I-125
approved_indications: Plaque irradiation of UM in the document’s comparison of radiation modalities.

therapies_index.name: LINAC (SRT)
approved_indications: Fractionated stereotactic radiation therapy for UM in the document’s comparison of radiation modalities.

therapies_index.name: CyberKnife (SRS)
approved_indications: Radiosurgery for UM in the document’s comparison of radiation modalities.

therapies_index.name: carbon
therapies_index.mechanism: The document suggests that sharper physical beam characteristics could reduce integral and normal-tissue doses; it does not establish a clinical advantage.
approved_indications: Ocular particle irradiation discussed as an alternative to OPT.

therapies_index.name: helium
therapies_index.mechanism: The document suggests that sharper physical beam characteristics could reduce integral and normal-tissue doses; it does not establish a clinical advantage.
approved_indications: Ocular particle irradiation discussed as a subject for further study.

therapies_index.name: FLASH
therapies_index.administration: Described as ultrahigh dose rate irradiation and identified for future study.

therapies_index.name: tantalum marker (clips) ocular surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Markers placed near the tumor provide references for target definition and precise alignment to the treatment beam.
approved_indications: Target delineation, planning, and image-guided positioning for OPT.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical placement of tantalum markers near the tumor border, accompanied by operative measurements.
key_toxicities: Short-term surgical complications include perforation, diplopia, and postoperative hemorrhage.
Tantalum markers can produce conjunctival granuloma.
monitoring: Use x-ray imaging of the markers for positioning verification.

therapies_index.name: clipless treatment
approved_indications: An option used by some centers for selected anterior tumors, including iris melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: Positioning can use clinical landmarks with a light field or a beam’s eye view camera. At the treatment team’s discretion, a larger margin, such as an additional 1 mm circumferentially, can address set-up uncertainty.
monitoring: Clinical assessment of positioning is needed when markers are not used.

therapies_index.name: enucleation
approved_indications: An option when severe inflammatory radiation toxicity cannot be managed adequately with other interventions.

therapies_index.name: laser ablation
approved_indications: Treatment of toxic tumor syndrome.

therapies_index.name: transscleral or transretinal ablation
approved_indications: Ablation of an irradiated tumor to treat toxic tumor syndrome.

therapies_index.name: antiangiogenic therapy
approved_indications: Prevention of toxic tumor syndrome.

therapies_index.name: steroids
approved_indications: Treatment of severe inflammatory toxicities after radiation therapy, when appropriate.

therapies_index.name: anti-VEGF therapy
approved_indications: Treatment of selected patients with complications after ocular irradiation.
Treatment of severe inflammatory radiation toxicities when appropriate.
Prophylactic use by some teams to reduce anterior-segment neovascularization.
Treatment of neovascular glaucoma.
Treatment of radiation maculopathy in an attempt to preserve vision and microcirculation.
therapies_index.administration: The document reports a prophylactic schedule used by some teams of 1£/2 months for 6 months then 1£/3 months.

therapies_index.name: vitrectomy
approved_indications: Treatment of severe inflammatory radiation toxicities when appropriate.

therapies_index.name: endoresection
approved_indications: Treatment of severe inflammatory radiation toxicities when appropriate.

therapies_index.name: laser treatment
approved_indications: Treatment of neovascular glaucoma once the ischemic retina has reattached.

therapies_index.name: clip removal
approved_indications: Correction of a conjunctival granuloma caused by a tantalum marker.

therapies_index.name: limbal stem cell transplantation
approved_indications: Studied in the setting of whole anterior segment irradiation for extensive iris seeding.

therapies_index.name: dilating drops
therapies_index.mechanism: Dilation may reduce the target area when treating iris melanomas.
approved_indications: Potential reduction of the irradiation target area for iris melanomas.
therapies_index.administration: Drops; no dosing schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: eyelid retraction
therapies_index.mechanism: Moving the eyelid outside the treatment field reduces its radiation exposure.
approved_indications: Reduction of eyelid toxicity during OPT.
therapies_index.administration: May involve retractors, head tilt, and chair rotation; for larger tumors, the upper eyelid is preferably fully retracted.

therapies_index.name: transpalpebral treatment
approved_indications: An alternative treatment approach that may be used strategically, including when treating larger tumors.
therapies_index.administration: Radiation is delivered through the eyelid.

therapies_index.name: wedge filters
therapies_index.mechanism: Beam shaping can reduce dose to posterior ocular structures or reduce the treated dose volume.
approved_indications: Normal-tissue dose optimization during OPT planning.
therapies_index.administration: Placed on patient collimators when included in a treatment plan.

therapies_index.name: notched aperture beams
therapies_index.mechanism: A locally reduced aperture margin can spare dose at the optic disc, macula, or optic nerve.
approved_indications: Sparing of posterior critical structures during OPT.
therapies_index.administration: Delivered through an aperture shaped with a localized notch.

conditions.name: uveal melanoma (UM)
conditions.description: An ocular malignancy for which proton therapy is an established treatment. Treatment planning must account for tumor dimensions, location relative to the optic disc and macula, and nearby tissues.

subtypes.name: iris melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An anterior tumor that may be positioned for treatment using visible clinical landmarks without tantalum clips in selected cases.

subtypes.name: ciliary body melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An anterior tumor for which a sharp distal beam fall-off can help spare posterior structures.

subtypes.name: choroidal melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Fundus autofluorescence, fluorescein angiography, and indocyanine green angiography can contribute to its differentiation from choroidal nevus, hemangioma, or metastasis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish tumor boundaries and assess structures relevant to treatment planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During ocular proton therapy evaluation and surgical marker placement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis and show the tumor's location and approximate shape relative to ocular anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During clinical assessment and target delineation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Geometrically accurate delineation requires registration that accounts for the camera. Prominent lateral or anterior tumors can obscure part of the tumor base, and optical distortion can affect geometric accuracy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure tumor base, height, and distance to the optic disc; assist diagnosis of small melanomas.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnosis and treatment planning, including successive examinations of a small suspected melanoma.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An increase in tumor size on 2 successive examinations is often decisive for diagnosing a small melanoma.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish choroidal nevus, melanoma, hemangioma, and metastasis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist diagnosis and locate the macula relative to the optic disc for registration of fundus images with the eye model.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning; for posterior tumors, it can support precise measurement of the distance from the tumor margin to the optic disc and/or macula.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize eye and tumor geometry and, after marker surgery, locate the clips; assess the dosimetric effect of silicone oil or gas tamponade when relevant.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When used for three-dimensional treatment planning or assessment of tamponade effects.

diagnostic_workup.test: Three-Tesla MRI with a surface coil
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Visualize three-dimensional tumor extent, adjacent tissues, small invasions into structures such as the optic nerve, and clips.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As complementary imaging for treatment planning; it may be especially useful for anterior or mushroom-shaped tumors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Eye motion during longer scans can produce artifacts. Flat tumor components may be difficult to delineate, so high spatial resolution alone does not establish the full tumor extent.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Delineate the tumor for most ocular proton therapy planning applications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During MRI-based treatment planning.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document identifies these images as providing the best distinction between tumor and retinal detachment for most planning purposes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Aid differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When MRI is used for differential diagnostic assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist clip localization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clips need to be identified on MRI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Susceptibility artifacts limit their suitability for accurate measurements.

diagnostic_workup.test: Surgical assessment and tantalum marker measurements
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish tumor and marker positions for target definition and image-guided treatment, including marker-to-limbus, marker-to-marker, and marker-to-tumor distances.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When tantalum marker placement is undertaken before ocular proton therapy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings such as flat or extraocular extension, variable pigmentation, and intraoperative complications can affect delineation and planning.

long_term_effects: Potential ocular proton therapy complications include eyelid inflammation or irritation, permanent eyelash loss, scleral telangiectasias, tear-duct occlusion, dry eyes, cataracts, pseudorecurrence associated with tumor inflammation, neovascular proliferation, secondary glaucoma, retinopathy, maculopathy, and optic neuropathy.
The document describes corneal limbal stem cell failure, eyelid or scleral necrosis, and exudative retinal detachment as generally rare severe radiation toxicities.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Published studies cited in the document report approximately 96% local control at 5 years, maintained at 10 and 15-year followup, and approximately 90% eye preservation at 5 years. Vision preservation depends in part on tumor size, proximity to the optic disc and macula, beam characteristics, planning, and ophthalmic care. Metastatic disease remains a concern for high-risk patients. After reirradiation for local failure, reported eye preservation is 40% at 5 years, with visual acuity of ≥20/200 preserved in 30% of patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with UM being considered for eye-preserving radiation treatment.
decision_rules: Use clinical examination and ophthalmic imaging to define the tumor; tantalum markers placed near its boundary usually support planning and positioning.
Choose gaze direction, target margins and beam shaping according to tumor dimensions, location and proximity to structures important for vision.
Consider patient preference and local availability when choosing among radiation modalities. Comparisons with other modalities are affected by differences in the tumors selected for treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: An established treatment for UM that aims to control the tumor while preserving the eye. Planning prioritizes tumor coverage and limits dose to healthy ocular structures.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies cited in the review report UM local control of approximately 96% at 5 years, maintained at 10 and 15-year followup, and eye preservation of approximately 90% at 5 years. The separate modality overview reports 5-year tumor control of 90%-99% and eye preservation of >90% for protons.

alternative_regimens.name: Ru-106
alternative_regimens.summary: Plaque brachytherapy is another irradiation modality. The modality overview reports UM tumor control of 80%-98% and eye preservation of >90% after 5 years; these are not outcomes from a direct comparison of equivalent patient groups.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Plaques are generally used for tumors with a smaller base and/or height and for tumors farther from the optic disc and macula; patient preference and local availability also affect modality choice.

alternative_regimens.name: I-125
alternative_regimens.summary: Plaque brachytherapy is another irradiation modality. The modality overview reports UM tumor control of 82%-99% and eye preservation of »90% after 5 years; these are not outcomes from a direct comparison of equivalent patient groups.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Plaques are generally used for tumors with a smaller base and/or height and for tumors farther from the optic disc and macula; patient preference and local availability also affect modality choice.

alternative_regimens.name: LINAC (SRT)
alternative_regimens.summary: Fractionated stereotactic radiation therapy is another modality. The modality overview reports UM tumor control of 85%-96% and eye preservation of »78% after 5 years.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Stereotactic radiation therapy is provided where established techniques are unavailable and/or because of patient circumstances.

alternative_regimens.name: CyberKnife (SRS)
alternative_regimens.summary: Single-fraction radiosurgery is another modality. The modality overview reports UM tumor control of 71%-84% and eye preservation of »81% after 5 years.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Stereotactic radiation therapy is provided where established techniques are unavailable and/or because of patient circumstances.

supportive_care: Plan around the optic disc and nerve, macula, retina, lens, ciliary body, cornea, limbus, lacrimal structures and eyelids to limit anticipated adverse effects.

Following irradiation, manage complications according to the affected tissue; options discussed include steroids, anti-VEGF therapy, vitrectomy and endoresection, with enucleation sometimes necessary.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Visual preservation depends in part on tumor size, its distance from the optic disc and macula, and beam penumbra. Historical clinical outcomes predominantly reflect dedicated treatment systems and should not automatically be assumed for beamlines with different characteristics.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose tumor is near the optic disc and/or macula.
decision_rules: Assess dose to the macula and optic disc or nerve while maintaining tumor coverage; sparing either structure may help preserve vision even when the other receives a higher dose.
Individualize gaze angle, lateral margins, aperture, distal range and, where appropriate, wedges or compensators.
Consider an aperture notch to reduce dose locally to the optic disc, macula or nerve.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Deliver a plan tailored to the proximity of vision-critical structures, using a sharply conformal beam and available normal-tissue-sparing techniques.

supportive_care: Evaluate dose-volume parameters for the macula and optic nerve when optimizing the plan and estimating the risk of vision loss.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reports cited by the authors identify macular volume and optic nerve length receiving 50% of the total dose ("V50%" or »28-30 Gray equivalent) as independent predictors of vision loss after OPT. The relevance of historical dose-volume data to contemporary 3D plans remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with an anterior tumor for whom marker surgery may be unsuitable because of comorbidities, extremely thin sclera or, rarely, patient preference; this includes suitable tumors with visible anterior chamber extension.
decision_rules: When tantalum markers are not used, position the eye using visible anatomic landmarks and a light field representing the radiation entrance field, or a beam’s eye view camera.
The treatment team may enlarge the margin to account for set-up uncertainty.
Consider dilating drops to reduce the area targeted for iris melanoma.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat an appropriate anterior tumor using a gaze and beam arrangement that limits dose to posterior ocular structures.

alternative_regimens.name: clipless treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Selected centers position patients for treatment without tantalum markers, using a light field or beam’s eye view camera.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Applicable to selected anterior tumors when clips are unsuitable or when the center uses this approach.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Typical planning target volume margins are 2 to 3 mm; the team may add, for example, an additional 1 mm circumferentially for uncertainty in a clipless set-up. Clipless positioning does not generally achieve the clip-based accuracy as readily for posterior intraocular tumors.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with an anterior ciliary body tumor, including selected small tumors with visible anterior chamber extension.
decision_rules: Use the sharp distal decline in dose to limit exposure of the optic disc and macula.

If marker surgery is unsuitable, selected anterior tumors may be positioned using clinical landmarks and a light field; consider a larger margin for set-up uncertainty at the treatment team’s discretion.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Plan proton irradiation to cover the anterior tumor while limiting dose to posterior structures.

supportive_care: Review ciliary body dose when planning to reduce the risk of neovascular glaucoma.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The review identifies MRI as potentially especially valuable for anterior tumors because ultrasound measurements may be inaccurate and intraoperative assessment may overestimate tumor extent.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with extensive iris seeding requiring irradiation of the whole anterior segment.
decision_rules: Account for the risk to the limbal stem cells when planning whole anterior segment irradiation.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: The review describes irradiation of the whole anterior segment for extensive iris seeding.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Limbal stem cell transplantation has been studied in this setting; the review does not establish it as routine treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with local failure following prior ocular proton therapy.
decision_rules: A further course of proton therapy can be considered as an eye-preserving salvage approach rather than enucleation.

recommended_regimens.name: ocular proton therapy (OPT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Repeat proton irradiation has provided local control and preservation of the eye in patients treated again after local failure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: After UM reirradiation, reported ocular preservation is 40% at 5 years, and visual acuity of ≥20/200 is preserved in 30% of patients.

alternative_regimens.name: enucleation
alternative_regimens.summary: Surgical removal of the eye is the comparator to eye-preserving salvage discussed by the authors.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The review notes that recurrence is rare after OPT and may follow a marginal or geographic miss or an in-field failure in a potentially radioresistant tumor.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with conjunctival tumors receiving ocular irradiation.

document_sections.heading: PTCOG Ocular Statement: Expert Summary of Current Practices and Future Developments in Ocular Proton Therapy
document_sections.content: Ocular tumors are uncommon but can impair vision and quality of life and may shorten life expectancy. Ocular proton therapy (OPT) is an effective treatment. The Particle Therapy Co-Operative Ocular Group presents an evidence- and expert-based assessment of current practice and future development. Comparisons of dosimetry and clinical outcomes across OPT systems are needed to guide planning, establish good practice, and define benchmarks for eye retention, vision, and quality of life. Prospective studies in selected groups, including patients with tumors near the optic disc and/or macula, may clarify differences among radiation modalities and beamlines in delivery, penumbra, tumor control, normal-tissue complications, and cost-effectiveness. Successful treatment has relied on combined ophthalmic imaging, ophthalmologist assessment, marker surgery, and radiation planning. Use of three-dimensional computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging is expected to increase, although spatial resolution may limit detection of flat, diffuse tumor extensions. Commercial ocular planning systems are being developed and may gain wider use. Sustaining OPT will require maintaining or upgrading older dedicated low-energy facilities, retaining shared degraded beamlines at large proton centers, and developing gantry beams with sufficient conformity. The first approach may produce the sharpest beams and least exposure of healthy tissue; the latter approaches may offer stronger long-term technical support and opportunities for innovation. Adequate patient volume and close, mutually informed collaboration among medical physics, ophthalmology, and radiation therapy are essential to an effective service.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Although ocular cancers are rare, they can threaten sight, quality of life, and potentially survival. Proton radiation therapy (RT) is associated with excellent local control and eye retention in malignant and benign ocular disease. The Particle Therapy Co-Operative Ocular Group (PTCOG Ocular) brings together institutions internationally that use proton or other particle beams for ocular tumors. Disease rarity and the substantial growth of proton centers over the past decade make evidence-informed, expert-consensus practice statements particularly important for appropriate, high-quality care. This report reviews current practice and findings from the second global multi-institutional survey presented at the inaugural PTCOG International Ocular Proton Therapy Symposium. It combines established research, expert views, and selected survey findings to provide patient-centered benchmarks, examine variation in practice, and support future research. Work on existing and new beamlines should prioritize patients’ outcomes and experiences, including local control, vision, and quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Indications for Ocular Proton Therapy
document_sections.content: Peer-reviewed evidence supports proton therapy as an established treatment for uveal melanoma (UM) and other ocular tumors. Since 1975, approximately 47,000 ocular patients worldwide have received particle-beam treatment for UM, conjunctival tumors, choroidal metastases, hemangiomas, other vascular tumors, macular degeneration, or retinoblastomas. Treatment has been primary, salvage, or adjuvant within combined-modality care. Published UM studies report approximately 96% local control at 5 years, sustained at 10 and 15-year followup, and approximately 90% eye preservation at 5 years. In selected cases, sight can be retained through careful gaze-angle and margin planning and postirradiation ophthalmic care; feasibility depends on tumor dimensions, proximity to the optic disc and macula, and beam penumbra. Metastatic disease remains problematic in high-risk patients, while immunotherapy options and therapeutic targets continue to be investigated. Recurrence after OPT is uncommon and may reflect a marginal or geographic miss or failure within a potentially radioresistant tumor. Published experience indicates that another course of OPT can provide acceptable local control and eye retention.

document_sections.heading: Target Volume Definition: Imaging and Surgical Best Practices
document_sections.content: OPT target definition generally combines clinical assessment and ophthalmic imaging with surgical placement of tantalum markers near the tumor edge. More recently, three-dimensional (3D) radiologic imaging, especially magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), has supplied complementary planning information. The illustrated imaging examples show how fundus images, MRI, CT, ocular coherence tomography, and ultrasound depict tumor location, anatomy, dimensions, and relationships to the macula and optic disc.

document_sections.heading: Ophthalmic imaging
document_sections.content: Fundus imaging (FI) is a principal diagnostic and OPT target-definition tool in standard clinical assessment. Available systems range from composites of small images to 200-degree ultra-wide-angle false-color imaging. They give indirect information about tumor shape and its relation to ocular anatomy, but geometrically accurate delineation requires registration to the eye model that accounts for the camera used. For prominent lateral or anterior tumors, the apex can hide the posterior portion of the tumor base. Optical distortion and the simple 2-point registration commonly used by treatment-planning systems (TPS) can also produce geometric discrepancies. A more advanced method registers FI to a digitally reconstructed MRI fundus. Fundus autofluorescence, fluorescein angiography, and indocyanine green angiography are used mainly to distinguish choroidal nevus, melanoma, hemangioma, and metastasis. Ocular coherence tomography can assist diagnosis and locate the macula relative to the optic disc for FI registration. In posterior tumors, the separation of the tumor edge from the optic disc and/or macula can be measured precisely. Ultrasound often settles the diagnosis of small melanomas by documenting growth across 2 successive examinations. It is the standard method for measuring tumor base and height and distance to the optic disc. At many OPT centers, ultrasound, FI, and intraoperative caliper findings supply the principal planning measurements. Table 1 compares which intraocular measurements are possible with the different modalities and identifies measurements whose applicability depends on the patient or device.

document_sections.heading: Tantalum marker placement and planning target volume definition
document_sections.content: Tantalum marker surgery and caliper measurements provide important inputs for OPT planning and image-guided delivery. Surgical assessment may document the tumor and markers in fundus or iris drawings and intraoperative photographs; marker-to-marker, marker-to-limbus, and marker-to-tumor distances; distances to the optic disc and macula; tumor base and height; clock-hour extent; and axial eye length. Communicating suspected extension, flat diffuse or extraocular spread, or pigmentation that impairs transillumination, including nevus of Ota and ocular melanocytosis, can improve planning. Silicone oil tamponade, vitreous hemorrhage, exudative retinal detachment, and other intraoperative events may affect delineation, margins, evaluation of critical structures, and possible gaze angles. Experienced ophthalmologic placement of markers is important for locating tumor boundaries accurately and avoiding surgical pitfalls. Markers near a tumor support planning margins and alignment to the beam at submillimeter accuracy. Typical planning target volume margins are 2 to 3 mm. Avoiding marker surgery altogether could improve comfort, lower cost, and remove surgical risks. It may not be advisable for some patients because of comorbidities, extremely thin sclera, or, rarely, patient preference. In these circumstances, clinicians can align to anatomic landmarks and a light field that reproduces beam entry, for example in iris or small ciliary body melanoma with visible anterior-chamber extension. The treatment team may add a larger margin for set-up uncertainty, such as an additional 1 mm circumferentially. Some centers already treat selected anterior tumors, including iris melanoma, without clips, using a light field or beam’s-eye-view camera. Achieving comparable accuracy without clips is harder for posterior intraocular tumors. Despite work on noninvasive anterior-segment video localization, x-ray imaging of clips remains the most accurate and dependable positioning method. Iris-pattern analysis is a promising noninvasive way to assess eye torsion. Inclusion of MRI, operative assessment, and FI is advised for target definition. MRI can be particularly informative for anterior tumors because ultrasound dimensions may be inaccurate and intraoperative assessment may overestimate extent. For mushroom-shaped tumors, it depicts 3D shape beyond conventional 1D measurements; MRI-based OPT planning therefore appears promising.

document_sections.heading: Treatment Planning
document_sections.content: OPT planning aims to cover the tumor while optimizing exposure of normal tissue. Imaging-derived eye and tumor models, treatment-planning software, and adjustments to beam shape and gaze direction support those aims.

document_sections.heading: Three-dimensional imaging
document_sections.content: Use of 3D imaging in OPT planning is increasing. OCTOPUS and the RayOcular module of RayStation (RaySearch Laboratories) can incorporate computed tomography (CT) and/or MRI into eye modeling or clinical target volume definition. CT depicts eye and tumor geometry and, if acquired after surgery, marker positions. It can establish or refine a geometric eye model, align that model to the scan, and assess how silicone oil or gas tamponade affects proton dose. Three-Tesla MRI with a surface coil is recommended for ocular imaging because its resolution can reveal small tumor invasions into neighboring structures, including the optic nerve. Submillimeter-resolution volumetric sequences show the tumor, adjacent tissues, and markers in 3D and permit comparison with conventional ophthalmic measurements. Longer acquisitions can introduce eye-motion artifacts, so high spatial resolution alone does not establish tumor extent. MRI protocols should reflect whether imaging is for diagnosis, planning, or followup. Diffusion and Perfusion Weighted Imaging are valuable for differential diagnosis; for most OPT planning, contrast-enhanced 3D T1-weighted imaging is preferred because it best differentiates tumor from retinal detachment. Gradient-echo sequences can assist marker localization but susceptibility artifacts make them unsuitable for precise measurements. MRI and ultrasound measurements of dimensions generally agree, and MRI and intraoperative marker-to-tumor measurements agreed satisfactorily in the majority of cases. Flat tumor components may nevertheless be difficult to distinguish on MRI, supporting incorporation of FI and operative findings. EYEPLAN was created in the 1980s for the small, mobile eye and its nearly uniform tissue composition. It constructs a spherical or ellipsoid model from axial eye length and limbus diameter, fits it to orthogonal x-ray-derived marker positions, and forms a 3D tumor volume from a fundus- or iris-plane base contour and the apex. Current versions can coregister FI, but CT and MRI information can be incorporated only indirectly; dose distributions and dose-volume histograms are calculated by ray tracing. OCTOPUS, developed through collaboration among the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB), and Charité − Universitätsmedizin Berlin, was the first TPS to incorporate 3D imaging fully. It retains a conventional EYEPLAN approach while fitting a predefined elliptical model to CT/MRI and using a rapid ray-tracing dose algorithm. Reported tumor control with OCTOPUS plans matches EYEPLAN plans. Image-based planning takes longer, although its models appear more realistic for some patients. More than 90% of OPT patients to date (»42,000 cases) were planned with EYEPLAN; two centers use Eclipse Ocular Proton Planning (EOPP, Varian Medical Systems), its commercial equivalent, and >3500 patients were planned with OCTOPUS. Development of EYEPLAN, EOPP, and OCTOPUS has stopped. RayOcular became clinically available in 2021; it combines EYEPLAN and OCTOPUS features in a contemporary environment and uses a pencil beam algorithm that produces more accurate dose distributions. Gantry- or scanning-based OPT systems use commercial TPS with CT/MRI planning, but lack coregistered FI for tumor definition. Manual transfer of all ophthalmologic 2D imaging findings into contours makes their planning difficult. The planning examples illustrate FI- and MRI-based contours, marker locations, dose distributions, and how a wedge or a sharp distal dose fall-off can spare posterior structures.

document_sections.heading: Critical structure dose optimization/planning best practices
document_sections.content: Planning prioritizes full tumor coverage alongside normal-tissue dose optimization. Ray-traced dose can be viewed on the fundus, in selected planes, and through dose-volume histograms (DVHs) for at-risk structures. Planning specifies collimator shape and any wedge, proton range and modulation, gaze angle, and marker positions for x-ray verification. Adjusting lateral margins, aperture, distal range, gaze, compensators, or wedges can improve eye and vision preservation. Structures should be evaluated systematically: posterior optic disc/nerve, macula, and retina; anterior lens, ciliary body, cornea, and limbus/limbal stem cells; and lacrimal gland, tear ducts, eyelids and eyelashes, and bony orbit. Automated gaze-angle selection is being explored. DVHs support optimization and complication-risk estimates. Several reports identify the volume of macula and length of optic nerve receiving 50% of the total dose, termed V50% or »28-30 Gray equivalent, as independent predictors of visual loss after OPT. Relatively sparing either the macula or optic disc may help preserve vision even if the other receives more dose. A narrow penumbra and suitable planning and delivery techniques are therefore important; an aperture notch can locally spare the disc, macula, or nerve. DVH review and ciliary-body and optic-disc/nerve dose adjustments can reduce neovascular glaucoma risk, while lens dose adjustment can limit cataract risk. Historical DVH and follow-up findings derive almost entirely from one planning system with simplified geometric anatomy; their applicability to modern segmentation based on 3D images is uncertain. A sharp distal dose fall-off permits irradiation of ciliary-body and iris tumors without irradiating the disc or macula. Wedges may reduce disc dose or treated volume, and dilating drops may shrink the iris melanoma target area. Limbal stem cell transplantation has been studied when extensive iris seeding requires irradiation of the whole anterior segment. Selecting gaze angle and systematically retracting eyelids help reduce long-term lid toxicity, including possible upper palpebral conjunctival keratinization. Transpalpebral irradiation can also be used strategically, and gaze may be optimized further to limit lacrimal-gland, tear-duct, and other exposure. Illustrated techniques include eyelid retraction, a macular aperture notch, a wedge, and a compensator.

document_sections.heading: OPT Delivery
document_sections.content: The document describes dedicated and shared beam systems, proton generation and shaping, patient positioning, and the dosimetry and quality assurance needed for highly conformal ocular irradiation.

document_sections.heading: Dedicated low-energy, dedicated high-energy, and nondedicated delivery systems
document_sections.content: Over the past 4 decades, most ocular treatments have come from a few pioneering centers using accelerators and beamlines adapted specifically for eye treatment. These include dedicated high- and low-energy systems. Low-energy machines have the sharpest physical dose characteristics because they require little beam degradation and permit individualized collimation; adequate beam current allows irradiation lasting <1 minute. The low incidence of OPT indications, expense of fully dedicated equipment, limited supply of modern low-energy clinical machines, withdrawal of dedicated eyeline vendors for high-energy systems, and aging accelerators create uncertainty about future beam provision. New centers may attach a dedicated nozzle to a high-energy accelerator or adapt high-energy gantries with ocular nozzles, couch or inclined positioning, and on-board imaging. High-energy beams must be slowed to treat intraocular tumors, widening distal fall-off and lateral penumbra. An in silico analysis indicates that resulting loss of conformity could increase normal-tissue injury and radiation effects. A survey obtained beam measurements from 5 dedicated low-energy and 14 high-energy systems. Median distal fall-off was 1.0 mm (0.9-1.2 mm) for low-energy systems and 2.8 mm (1.5-6.0 mm) for high-energy systems; the parentheses give reported ranges. Median lateral penumbra was 1.4 mm (1.2-1.9 mm) and 1.6 mm (1.2-3.0 mm), respectively. High-energy solutions differ significantly in dosimetric properties. Careful engineering can partly offset degradation, yielding some parameters close to dedicated low-energy systems, but energy selection substantially lowers beam fluence and increases treatment time. Future comparisons must determine how distal and lateral penumbra, dose heterogeneity, range uncertainty, beam angle, and marker placement influence normal-tissue doses, eye loss, vision change, retinopathy, glaucoma, eyelid effects, and other outcomes. Nearly all current clinical follow-up evidence comes from dedicated OPT systems, so beam properties are especially important when expanding treatment to universal beamlines.

document_sections.heading: Beam generation
document_sections.content: Ocular proton beams can come from low-energy isochronous cyclotrons operating at 60-74 MeV with locally developed eyelines; high-energy isochronous cyclotrons such as Varian ProBeam and IBA Proteus 235; high-energy synchrocyclotrons such as IBA S2C2 and Mevion S250i; or synchrotrons selectable down to 70 MeV, such as Hitachi-V ProBeat 250, Optivus, and Siemens. Synchrocyclotrons may have lower dose rates and longer treatment times. An AVO-Light proton linac is in development, with selectable 70 to 200 MeV energy, a small footprint, and narrow beam emittance. Most centers are based in hospitals or clinical research institutes. Table 2 surveys centers, equipment, beam characteristics, and treatment rooms, including dedicated eye rooms, shared gantries with eye-adapted nozzles, and rooms shared with another treatment line. More than half of operational OPT systems were developed in house; a minority came from commercial vendors. Most use a rotating range-modulator wheel to create the spread-out-Bragg-peak (SOBP). Wheel-library sizes vary, including 12 at UFHPTI, 40 at MGH, and >90 at CCC. Other SOBP approaches use active energy selection or stacking, sometimes with a ridge filter. Final range adjustment can use a discrete shifter, a continuous shifter such as a variable water column, a selectable wedge, or a smoothly varying-thickness wheel. Experience places useful OPT energies at 65 to 75 MeV (from 36 to 46 mm in water), accommodating the deepest tumors, overlying tissues, margins, and compensators. A high-energy accelerator can achieve ocular energy using absorbers and slits in an energy selection system (ESS) or machine adjustment; machine-adjusted systems still need fine range shifters at the eyeline. Energy-adjustment resolution depends on system design and local clinical preference. Degraded high-energy gantries and some fixed horizontal lines permit beam ranges >36 mm and potentially lateral approaches through the zygomatic bone. Multiple anterior fields are being planned to decrease anterior dose and improve robustness, but their longer delivery and possible adverse effects from multiple anterior and lateral entry paths must be considered. Planners should account for dose shadows behind clips lying anterior to the tumor. Multiple-gantry-field optimization and landmark-based positioning are under investigation at NWMPC (Chicago). Comparisons across beamlines must assess tumor control, eye preservation, visual loss, functional and aesthetic quality of life, and costs.

document_sections.heading: Beam shaping
document_sections.content: Individualized collimators and compensators are costly. Common maximum aperture diameters of 30 to 35 mm balance uniformity against adequate dose rate. Patient-specific brass collimators are used universally but demand labor and special disposal. Microleaf collimation is technically feasible but unavailable at present. Fabricated mesh or microhole collimators for spatially fractionated proton therapy aim to lower anterior exposure and eyelid toxicity; 3D-printed polylactic-acid collimators and compensators have also been developed. Gantry-adapted systems can form 40 to 60 mm fields with several pencil beams, suitable for conjunctival tumors without patching fields. Vendor high-energy systems commonly use pencil beam scanning, either across an aperture or with several adjacent beams for larger areas. Their ocular dose fall-off and penumbra are generally wider than dedicated beamlines because of energy and fluence losses in the ESS and nozzle absorber dimensions and proximity. Low ESS efficiency also affects dose rate and treatment duration. Approximately a third of centers use polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) or aluminum wedges on patient collimators to spare posterior tissue and reduce treated volume; they are particularly useful with sharply conformal isodoses. Small aperture notches can provide highly localized sparing of the optic disc and macula.

document_sections.heading: Patient set-up
document_sections.content: Most centers use comparable planning and delivery approaches, usually treating upright with a dedicated fixed beam; 3 centers use supine or inclined couches. Chairs and headframes permit adjustment in orthogonal directions and correction of pitch and yaw. All centers use orthogonal digital x-ray panels for simulation and positioning, although their arrangements differ. Maintaining the planned gaze direction requires patient participation and helps reduce radiation side effects. If pretreatment vision in the treated eye is poor, the other eye can fixate; clinical assessment must verify position and conjugate gaze. Eyelid exposure affects short- and long-term erythema, scarring, eyelash loss, keratinization, appearance, and quality of life. For small and medium tumors, clinicians can usually move most or all eyelid tissue out of the field by combining suitable retractors, expertise, head tilt, and chair rotation. For large tumors, full upper-lid retraction is preferred to limit keratinization; transpalpebral treatment is an alternative. Despite being iterative and invasive, positioning has been reported by OPT institutions to achieve submillimetric accuracy. Closed-circuit video, aided by infrared illumination, monitors eye motion during irradiation. Established dedicated programs average 100 to 300 patients annually. Gantries fitted with ocular nozzles are expected to treat fewer patients individually but could improve access and reduce travel because gantries are more widely available.

document_sections.heading: Dosimetry and quality assurance
document_sections.content: Sharp ocular particle beams, narrow fields, submillimetric range prescription, and linear energy transfer quenching at the Bragg peak place substantial demands on quality assurance (QA). A survey of 15 ocular particle-therapy institutions found varying QA procedures and calibration practices reflecting beamline and accelerator differences. Table 3 presents the surveyed frequencies for output, range, SOBP shape, lateral profile, dose rate, field coincidence, laser alignment, and safety-interlock checks. Most centers verify output and range daily. Approximately half check SOBPs and lateral profiles daily; others do so weekly or monthly. Daily QA takes from <15 minutes to more than an hour. Five centers use commercial devices to measure depth dose and range, while ten use custom equipment. A UCSF daily method uses a 3D-printed cone phantom and radiochromic film to assess range and x-ray-to-beam coincidence together in <5 minutes, with respective resolution within 0.1 and 0.2 mm. Half of centers use commercial equipment to measure lateral profiles. An ICPO 2D scintillator checks profile flatness, symmetry, and proton-to-light-field coincidence. Locally built devices can be precise and economical but need to match commercial systems in compactness, ease of use, speed, and analysis. All but one survey respondent follows the International Atomic Energy Agency TRS-398 Code of Practice for Dosimetry, although ion chambers and measurement media differ. Patient-field monitor units are determined in several ways: rapid ion-chamber verification in a plastic reference phantom; water measurements at 5 of 15 centers; measurements with a patient aperture at 3 of 15; or analytical models, look-up tables, databases, or TPS calculations. Most centers, 13 of 15, apply a constant relative biological effectiveness factor of 1.1 when converting physical to prescribed dose. One carbon center uses a TPS-calculated relative biological effectiveness. No center applied depth-dependent linear energy transfer corrections. American Association of Physicists in Medicine task-group reports do not address OPT specifically, but their methods are useful. TG-100 supports failure-mode analysis and extra checks for higher-risk light-field positioning without x-ray alignment. TG-224 covers machine QA for passive scattering and scanning, but its proposed §1 mm tolerances do not meet OPT precision requirements. TG-275 addresses staff chart-review checklists and automated plan checks. Some centers have consequently developed patient-specific software to select the range-modulator wheel, transfer aperture-manufacturing files, and estimate planned-field monitor units. Larger teams may improve service continuity, but assigning only a small share of each staff member’s time to ocular treatment can challenge consistent, safe QA. Variation in practice supports greater collaboration, standardization, and adoption of effective methods; clearer specifications may encourage OPT-specific vendor QA equipment.

document_sections.heading: Post-OPT Care Best Practices
document_sections.content: Definitive OPT produces high local-control rates but may cause eyelid inflammation or irritation, lasting eyelash loss, scleral telangiectasia, tear-duct blockage, dry eye, cataract, pseudorecurrence from tumor inflammation, neovascular proliferation, secondary glaucoma, retinopathy, maculopathy, and optic neuropathy. Generally uncommon severe radiation effects include limbal stem-cell failure, eyelid or scleral necrosis, and exudative retinal detachment. Short-term surgical harms include perforation, diplopia, and postoperative bleeding; tantalum markers can cause conjunctival granulomas. Particular attention to toxicity is warranted in adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients with UM. At PSI, 272 AYA patients aged <40 years were identified between 1997 and 2007, alongside 1984 treated adults. Despite excellent tumor control, meaningful complications included visual loss associated with neovascular glaucoma, maculopathy, optic neuropathy, retinopathy, cataracts, and dry eyes. Nearly 50% of AYA patients had tumors near the optic disc or macula; some retained sight despite high-dose RT. Selected patients can receive anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy. Treatment toxicity motivates more individualized, accurate models integrating MRI and fundus photographs to improve conformity and reduce late effects. Because planned doses can predict RT toxicity, surgical, planning, and delivery measures can limit dose to critical anatomy. Toxic tumor syndrome can be managed with laser, transscleral, or transretinal ablation of the irradiated tumor and prevented with antiangiogenic therapy. Depending on circumstances, severe inflammatory RT effects may respond to steroids, anti-VEGF, vitrectomy, or endoresection; enucleation is sometimes required. Some teams give preventive anti-VEGF, for example 1£/2 months for 6 months then 1£/3 months, to reduce anterior-segment neovascularization. Management of neovascular glaucoma includes antiVEGF and laser treatment after reattachment of ischemic retina. For radiation maculopathy, anti-VEGF may be used in an attempt to retain vision and microcirculation. Angio-ocular coherence tomography may improve mapping of the foveal avascular zone. Removing a clip readily resolves conjunctival granuloma. Local failures of UM and conjunctival tumors have been retreated with protons. After UM reirradiation, reported ocular preservation is 40% at 5 years and visual acuity of ≥20/200 is retained in 30% of patients, providing an effective salvage option compared with enucleation. Table 4 summarizes published 5-year tumor control and eye-preservation outcomes for proton treatment, Ru-106 and I-125 plaques, LINAC (SRT), and CyberKnife (SRS). Further study is needed; increasing attention is being paid to screening for earlier diagnosis, young adults and other distinct groups, targeted therapies, and immunotherapies.

document_sections.heading: Comparison with different radiation modalities
document_sections.content: Selection bias limits comparisons between protons and other radiation techniques. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews report that plaques generally treat tumors with smaller bases and/or heights and those farther from the optic disc or macula than proton-treated tumors. In these studies, short- and long-term local control generally favored charged particles over plaque brachytherapy, but their proton results came solely from dedicated low-energy systems. Stereotactic RT is described as the least often used option and is delivered where established approaches are unavailable or patient circumstances warrant it. For comparable tumors, reports describe more favorable normal-tissue doses and visual outcomes with OPT than other RT approaches. One reported comparison found less radiation retinopathy with protons, most likely because of more uniform dose and exposure of smaller retinal volumes. Local-control results for the alternative techniques vary more. Table 4 compares 5-year tumor control and eye preservation for UM across irradiation modalities. Anterior-eye complications occur more often with proton beams than with other radiation techniques, although their frequency is declining with contemporary planning, dosing, delivery, and specialist ophthalmic care. A United States cost analysis suggested that a short OPT course of 4-5 fractions may be more cost-effective than plaque brachytherapy under the insurance arrangements assessed. The finding cannot be generalized internationally: treatment costs and reimbursement depend strongly on national priorities and plaque availability. The comparative costs of plaques and photon stereotactic treatment arising from retinopathy, visits, visual loss, and other harms remain under investigation and may change cost-effectiveness assessments. Patient preference and local availability also influence clinical treatment choice.

document_sections.heading: Future Directions and Conclusions
document_sections.content: Further improvement in ocular care calls for better imaging, TPS, QA methods, and vendor options for low- and high-energy lines, together with reduced lateral penumbra and distal fall-off and improved dose uniformity and rate. The 2022 Second International Survey identified the leading development priorities summarized in Table 5: a sustainable commercial TPS; MRI and image fusion for outlining targets and normal tissue; better QA devices and more standardized practice; and wider OPT access. Eye tracking and gating, multi-institutional outcome research, clipless treatment, biological planning, multibeam and gantry-based approaches, FLASH irradiation, and helium and carbon particles were also identified for future research. Low demand and stringent technical requirements limit the commercial availability of dedicated ocular proton systems. Development must balance beam optimization, access, and cost. Excellent historic outcomes from dedicated facilities must not automatically be assumed for beams of different quality; new systems need evaluation to establish whether they reproduce those outcomes. Helium and carbon have shown local-control rates similar to OPT, while their sharper physical characteristics suggest a potential clinical advantage from lower integral and normal-tissue doses and fewer late effects. Better integration of images may improve eye-model accuracy and eventually eliminate markers from target definition and perhaps image guidance. Established centers’ high tumor-control rates leave little apparent opportunity to increase control, but more accurate models, sharp beams, and optimization across care may reduce adverse effects. Proton and heavier-particle treatment of ocular tumors has been studied extensively over decades. Delivering its potential for local control, lasting eye retention, and useful vision requires specialized clinical and physics expertise and careful application. Acute and late ocular morbidity depend on patient, tumor, and treatment characteristics, so further study of techniques and combined clinical approaches remains important for functional outcomes. Adequate patient throughput and strong collaboration among ophthalmology, RT, and medical physics are crucial to successful OPT care.
